notes.title: Chapter map: Automatic prompt optimization
notes.html:
How a program searches for prompt text against a metric, and when that is worth paying for. Note 63 says why reading outputs can't accept a change; 64 and 65 are the first scored searches; 66 is the compiler that made it a practice; 67 and 68 are the search with written feedback; 69 is how examples for middle steps get made; 71 prices a run, and 72 says what is left after a model change; 70 is a side route into the weights. Read each arrow as a sentence: DSPy is priced by cost-benefit.

Blue = SUPPORTING, yellow = BREADTH. This section has no CORE notes.

Reading order:63 why hand-tuning doesn't scale64 APE65 OPRO67 TextGrad68 evolutionary search66 DSPy69 few-shot bootstrapping71 cost-benefit72 portability70 distillation

Changed on 31 Oct 2026:

  • No tier changed and no note merged. The section stays 7 SUPPORTING and 3 BREADTH.
  • Two stages and badges moved from the index's default. Note 72 is ship, because it acts at a model change. Notes 64, 65 and 70 are ⚪ Fading, each naming its replacement.
  • The winner's curse has one home. Several older notes explained it; note 64 owns it.
  • Note 72 kept only what is specific to compiled prompts. The tuple stays in note 09, and the upgrade in note 87.

Older text of every note is in 08-Prompt-engineering/_superseded/07-Automatic Prompt Optimization/.

Which optimiser?

Before this tree comes note 71's tree: should you run one at all? The order follows DSPy's guide, as of Oct 2026.

  • ✍️ Hand-tune (63): if modules multiply beyond what a person can try, go on.
  • BootstrapFewShot (69): if the task has rules a few examples can't show, instruction search matters more.
  • GEPA (68): if you have no strong reflection model, or the run's cost is too high, use another.
  • MIPROv2 (66): if a task's demos matter little, instruction-only search is simpler.

At a glance

Not re-read in this pass: Promptfoo and other eval tools, which sit in the evaluation map.

Four bullets

  • The one big idea: an optimiser is a scored search, so it inherits every property of its metric and set. Build those first; they outlive every prompt the search produces.
  • The two most-confused pairs: a rewrite vs an optimisation (64: no score, nothing was selected) · a selection score vs a held-out score (64: the first chose the winner, so it can't measure it).
  • Ten minutes before an interview: note 66's compile and run split, note 71's tree and budget sum, note 64's Break it, note 72's upgrade path.
  • Cross-section links: the metric is a judge more often than not, and its biases get optimised too; compiled output is versioned in prompt versioning. Content gaps: no note on writing a metric that returns useful feedback, which GEPA needs; no measured evidence on portability beyond one row in one paper.

notes.title: Why Hand-Tuning Doesn't Scale — You Can Propose a Better Prompt, You Can't See That It Is Better
notes.html:
References

Khattab et al. 2023: DSPy · Opsahl-Ong et al. 2024: optimizing instructions and demonstrations for multi-stage programs · Sclar et al. 2023: sensitivity to spurious features in prompt design

TL;DR

Hand-tuning breaks in three places at once: the search space is a product, a read of twenty outputs is mostly noise, and each edit is an untested change to a coupled system. The fix is a fixed scored set, which an engineer can use with no optimiser at all. An optimiser is what that set makes possible; it isn't the point.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change
Flow:edit a promptread 20 outputsshipnoise and silent regressions accumulateevery candidate scored the same waya person or a program can search

Recall

Prompt Answer
Why is the space intractable? Instructions × example sets, multiplied across modules: a product, not a sum.
Why can't you judge by reading? At n = 20, p = 0.8, one standard error is about 9 points.
What comes first, the harness or the optimiser? The harness: a set and a metric are useful with no optimiser.

The idea

You edit a support prompt, read twenty outputs, and they look better. You ship. A month later a colleague undoes it. Nobody can say whether either edit helped, because reading twenty outputs can't separate a gain from a lucky sample.

Two abilities are mixed up here. Proposing a better prompt is something engineers do well, often better than a search. Knowing it is better needs a score on a fixed set, and no amount of experience replaces that.

Pipelines make it worse. Three modules that feed each other can't be tuned one at a time, because each is tuned against a neighbour you are about to change.

The trade: a fixed set and a metric cost days of work before any prompt improves; they buy every later edit a verdict, from a person or a program.

How it works

The hand-tuning loop has no memory and no measurement, so it wanders.

The two sums behind the argument. The noise sum is quoted from error bars and paired tests.

options per module = I · C(N, k)              ← I instructions, k demos from N examples
10 · C(200, 4)     = 646,849,500              ← one module
three modules      = that³ ≈ 2.7 × 10²⁶       ← nobody sweeps a product
SE at n = 20, p = 0.8 = √(0.8 · 0.2 / 20) ≈ 0.09
Rule What actually happens
The argument is about pipelines One short prompt has a small space, and a skilled person is competitive. The product appears when modules multiply.
Coupling is the real reason Modules feed each other, so tuning one against a fixed neighbour finds a local optimum (component vs end to end).

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026). The argument is the motivation of the DSPy and multi-stage papers, and vendors now ship scored optimisers (chapter map, Landscape).
  • Stronger-model test: partly. A stronger model reacts less to wording, so a phrasing search has less room. What won't change: a read of twenty outputs is the same noisy measurement on any model.

Code

The smallest thing that replaces reading: one score, same cases, every edit.

def score(render, call, cases, check):
    """render: prompt version; call: your model call; check: an assertion or a validated judge."""
    return sum(check(call(render(c["input"])), c) for c in cases) / len(cases)

Break it: the belief that a visible win after an edit means the edit helped. Both reads below use the same prompt.

import random
random.seed(7)
def read(p=0.80, n=20): return sum(random.random() < p for _ in range(n)) / n
trials = 100_000
b_wins = sum(read() - read() >= 0.10 for _ in range(trials)) / trials   # A and B are the same prompt
print(f"B 'beats' an identical A by 10+ points in {b_wins:.0%} of 20-output reads")
# look for: about one read in five showing a 10-point win for a change that did nothing
# naive belief predicts: almost none, because nothing changed

Run on Python 3.15, it prints 18%: a 10-point "win" with no change at all.

Measure it

  • Offline: the score of each edit against the live prompt on the same golden set, with the noise floor marked. Baseline: the live version.
  • In production: edits per prompt that carry an eval run, against those that don't. A prompt that keeps being edited with no run attached is being hand-tuned blind.
  • Enforced by: the CI gate, where a change with no passing run is not merged. Without it, this is a habit.

Interview

30-second answer: Three things break. The space is a product across modules, so nobody can sweep it. A read of twenty outputs has a standard error near nine points, so "looks better" is usually sampling. And each edit is an untested change to a coupled system. The fix is a fixed set and a metric. An optimiser becomes possible after that, but the set pays for itself first.

Q · Mechanism — Why is a pipeline harder than three separate prompts? Because the modules aren't separable. The rewrite step's output is the reasoning step's input, so tuning one against a frozen neighbour finds a local optimum for a neighbour you're about to change. The end-to-end pairs in your set also say nothing about what the middle step should emit. That's why multi-stage optimisers score the whole program and tune all modules together.

Q · Trade-off — A senior engineer says they can hand-tune better than any optimiser. Are they wrong? Often not, on proposing. The simpler rung is a person with a scored set, and they'll find structural fixes no search over wording can reach: a wrong framing, a missing constraint, a retrieval bug. Where the claim fails is on knowing. By reading they can't tell a four-point gain from noise. I'd climb to an optimiser only for a stable pipeline where the combinations exceed what a person can try.

Pitfalls

  • "We know these prompts well, so we don't need tooling"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the team has lived with the prompt for months and its outputs feel familiar.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: that knowledge sits in people, not in anything a new teammate or a new model can use. Nothing records why each clause exists.
    ↳ Think instead: the durable asset is the set and the metric; a prompt without them can't be re-derived.
  • Don't apply the combinatorics to a single prompt.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the product formula sounds universal, and it justifies a framework.
    ↳ What goes wrong: one short prompt has few real options, so you add a dependency and a compile step to search a space a person covers in an afternoon.
    ↳ Do instead: use the simpler rung, a person with a scored set, until modules multiply.
  • Don't use an optimiser to skip reading the failures.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a run feels more rigorous than reading fifty bad outputs by hand.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the search climbs the hill it is on. If the cause is missing context or a wrong decomposition, the best wording is still wrong.
    ↳ Do instead: classify failures first (failure taxonomy); only wording failures go to a search.
  • Not the same: hand-tuning as a first draft vs hand-tuning as maintenance
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: the title reads as if hand-tuning is always wrong.
    ↳ Difference: a person is the fastest route to a first version. What fails is relying on edits and reading to keep a live prompt healthy for months.
    ↳ Think instead: draft by hand, and maintain with a scored set.
  • Shelf life: the noise arithmetic is permanent. The size of the phrasing search shrinks as models get less sensitive to wording.

Connections

Path:eval-driven developmentwhy hand-tuning doesn't scaleAPEDSPycost-benefit
  • Builds on prompt sensitivity: why one score is one sample from a spread.
  • Measured by golden datasets: the fixed set every candidate is scored on.
  • Owned elsewhere: error bars and paired tests covers the statistics.
  • Used by APE: the smallest automated version of a scored search.
  • Drilled in hand-tune or auto-optimise.

notes.title: APE — Infer the Instruction, Score Every Candidate, Keep the Best
notes.html:
References

Zhou et al. 2022: Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers · Yang et al. 2023: OPRO · Opsahl-Ong et al. 2024: MIPRO

TL;DR

Show a model input-output pairs and ask what instruction produced them; do that many times to get a pool. Then run every candidate on a scored set and keep the highest. The generating is the cheap half. The scored selection is the method, and its top score is optimistic because it was selected.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change
Flow:5 input-output pairsa model infers an instructioncandidate poolscore each on a training splitkeep the bestcheck on a set the search never saw

Recall

Prompt Answer
What are the two halves? A model proposes instructions from examples; code scores each and takes the best.
Why is the winner's score too high? It is a maximum over many noisy scores: selection bias.
What is the method's result, with its model? Human-level on 24 of 24 tasks, text-davinci-002, 2023 version.

The idea

You ask a chat model to improve your prompt, it returns a confident rewrite, and you use it. That is hand-tuning with an extra step: nothing measured the rewrite.

APE changes two things. First, you stop describing the task. You show demonstrations and let a model infer the instruction, which helps because writing a task down precisely is the part people do badly, and most teams already have examples. Second, you never trust one candidate. You generate many and run each against labelled examples.

This is a request at proposal time and enforced at selection: the model may propose anything, and only the score decides.

The trade: you pay for candidates × examples model calls, and you get a winner whose score is inflated by the selection itself.

How it works

The method is a pool and a maximum. The last gate is yours to build.

Rule What actually happens
Selection is the score over a training split The paper's score is the expectation over training examples; the reported number comes from a separate test set.
Cheap filter first Score all candidates on a small subset, then re-score survivors on fresh subsets. Poor candidates never reach the whole set.
Iterative APE Ask for variants of the top scorers that keep their meaning, then re-score. It's a local search.

Evolution

Lineage:2022 greedy instruction induction (no scoring)Nov 2022 APE: a scored poolSep 2023 OPRO: scores fed back as contextJun 2024 MIPRO: proposals grounded in data and code
  • Maturity: ⚪ Fading (Oct 2026). APE as a named method is replaced by DSPy's optimisers; DSPy's list has no APE. Its scored-selection step is in every one of them.
  • Stronger-model test: yes for the proposer; current models write good candidates from a description. What won't change: a candidate is accepted by a score, and that maximum is biased.
  • Checked on: text-davinci-002 and GPT-3 sizes, 2022–23. Nothing here was re-run on current models.

Code

The paper's forward template, shortened. The examples carry the task.

① TASK     I gave a friend an instruction and five inputs.          ← frames the output as an instruction
② EXAMPLES Input: {{x1}} Output: {{y1}} … ×5                        ← the task, shown and not described
③ OUTPUT   The instruction was <COMPLETE>                           ← the model continues from here

Break it: the belief that the winner's score is what you'll get. Every candidate below has the same true accuracy.

import random, statistics as st
random.seed(7)
def score(p, n): return sum(random.random() < p for _ in range(n)) / n
TRUE, POOL, SEL, HELD = 0.75, 100, 50, 500        # every candidate is equally good
sel = [max(score(TRUE, SEL) for _ in range(POOL)) for _ in range(300)]
held = [score(TRUE, HELD) for _ in range(300)]
print(f"winner on the selection set: {st.mean(sel):.3f}, same winner held out: {st.mean(held):.3f}")
# look for: a winner 10+ points above its held-out score
# naive belief predicts: the top score is what you will get in production

Run on Python 3.15, it prints 0.894 and 0.749. A pool of 100 identical candidates scored on 50 examples "finds" 14 points that don't exist.

Measure it

  • Offline: held-out score of the winner against the prompt you'd otherwise ship, on a set the search never saw. Ignore the selection score. A gain inside the noise floor is no gain.
  • In production: the gap between the search's score and the held-out score, per run. A gap that grows as pools get larger is selection bias.
  • Enforced by: the held-out comparison in the release gate. The proposal step is a request; selection is code.

Interview

30-second answer: APE treats the instruction as something to search for. A model looks at input-output pairs and infers the instruction, you sample a pool of those, you run each on labelled examples and keep the top scorer. The paper's result is human-level on all 24 instruction-induction tasks, on text-davinci-002. The contribution is the scored selection, and the gotcha is that the winner's score is biased upward.

Q · Mechanism — Why does it need a separate set after selection? Because the maximum of many noisy scores picks the luckiest as well as the best. The more candidates you try, the worse that gets, so the selection score can't be reported. A set the search never touched gives an unbiased estimate of the one winner you chose.

Q · Trade-off — When would you still write this loop yourself? The simpler rung is a person writing three candidates and scoring them on a fixed set. A generated pool is the next step up: one prompt, some labelled examples, a metric, and perhaps fifty lines of code. I'd stop there for a single-prompt task. I'd move to a framework only for a multi-step pipeline, where the examples for intermediate steps don't exist yet.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Tasks at or above human level 24 of 24 zero-shot, Instruction Induction, InstructGPT (text-davinci-002), arXiv v2 and ICLR 2023 cited (paper)
The same, first preprint 19 of 24 arXiv v1, Nov 2022; the arXiv listing still shows it cited (paper)
Curated BIG-Bench tasks 17 of 21 same paper, same model cited (paper)
Interquartile mean 0.810 vs human 0.749 across the 24 tasks, v2; v1 reported 0.765 cited (paper)

Pitfalls

  • "APE is asking a model to improve my prompt"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the visible step is a model writing a prompt, and chat tools offer exactly that.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: that is the proposal half alone. Without scoring every candidate on labelled examples nothing was selected, so nothing was found.
    ↳ Think instead: no score, no optimisation: it's a rewrite.
  • "A strange-looking winner should be distrusted, a clean one trusted"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: readers treat fluent text as sound text.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: meaning and score are separate axes; prompt sensitivity shows scores moving on features with no meaning at all. Oddness tells you nothing either way.
    ↳ Think instead: let the held-out score decide, and read the prompt for review, not for proof.
  • Not the same: a training-split score vs a held-out score
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are accuracy on a set of labelled examples, and dashboards show one number.
    ↳ Difference: the first chose the winner, so it is biased. The second didn't, so it estimates what ships.
    ↳ Think instead: report only the score of a set that took no part in choosing.
  • Don't assume a zero-shot winner keeps winning with examples added.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a better instruction sounds additive.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the paper saw three tasks get worse when in-context examples were added to selected instructions, and suggests they had overfitted the zero-shot setting.
    ↳ Do instead: score the exact prompt you will ship, examples included.
  • Shelf life: the method's name is fading; the scored pool and the selection bias are not.

Connections

Path:why hand-tuning doesn't scaleAPEOPRODSPy
  • Builds on in-context learning: the examples are what the proposer conditions on.
  • Measured by golden datasets: the source of both the selection and the held-out set.
  • Owned elsewhere: error bars and paired tests covers how to read the gap.
  • Superseded by DSPy: same selection, grounded proposals, whole pipelines.

notes.title: OPRO — The Scores So Far Become the Optimiser's Prompt
notes.html:
References

Yang et al. 2023: Large Language Models as Optimizers · Zhou et al. 2022: APE · Opsahl-Ong et al. 2024: MIPRO

TL;DR

Put the instructions tried so far, each with its score, into a meta-prompt in ascending order, and ask for a new one that scores higher. The optimisation history is the context; there is no gradient, only a pattern the model continues. It gives APE a memory, and it spends a full evaluation to return one number per candidate.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change
Flow:top 20 instructions with scores, worst first+ 3 exemplarsmodel proposes 8score each on a fixed training sampleadd to the historybest instructiontest set

Recall

Prompt Answer
What is in the meta-prompt? Task, exemplars, instruction-score pairs ascending, and a request for a higher score.
Why ascending? The ablation found faster, better results; recency bias is the paper's hypothesis.
What does "up to 8%" mean? Best zero-shot on GSM8K, PaLM 2-L: 80.2 against "think step by step" 71.8.

The idea

APE samples a pool, and each candidate knows nothing of the last. If step-by-step instructions keep scoring higher than terse ones, the next sample can't use that.

OPRO writes that pattern into the prompt. The optimiser model reads which instructions scored what, and proposes one that continues the trend. It's the same scored selection, with memory.

Each proposal is a request; only your scorer accepts or rejects it.

The trade: you run many evaluation rounds and pay for a whole scored set each round, and each round returns only a number, not a reason.

How it works

The whole method is one prompt, rebuilt each step.

Rule What actually happens
Bounded history Only the best 20 instructions stay in the meta-prompt, because of the context limit.
Fixed training sample On GSM8K, 3.5% of the training set (about 261 examples), the same subset throughout.
Overfitting is measured Training accuracies were often 5–20 points above test. The paper keeps no validation set by default, after finding curves that move together on two BBH tasks.

Evolution

Lineage:Nov 2022 APE: a scored poolSep 2023 OPRO: scores in the contextJun 2024 module-level OPRO as a baseline for MIPROJul 2025 GEPA: reasons in place of numbers
  • Maturity: ⚪ Fading (Oct 2026). OPRO survives as a baseline and an idea; DSPy's list has no OPRO. GEPA replaces the score-only channel with text feedback.
  • Stronger-model test: yes. A wording search has less to find on models that care less about wording. What won't change: a bigger history can't fix a noisy score.
  • Checked on: PaLM 2-L, text-bison, gpt-3.5-turbo and gpt-4, 2023.

Code

The meta-prompt, shortened from the paper's Figure 3.

① TASK       I have some texts with scores, in ascending order.                 ← the frame
② CONTEXT    text: {{instruction}} score: {{0-100}} … best 20, ascending         ← the trajectory
③ EXAMPLES   input: Q: {{q}} A: <INS>  output: {{a}} … 3 exemplars               ← what it must handle
④ OUTPUT     Write a new text that is different and scores higher. In [ ].       ← parseable

Break it: the belief that history always helps. A scripted proposer stands in for the model.

import random, statistics as st
SIZE, STEPS, PER = 12, 25, 4                         # a prompt = 12 yes/no phrasing choices
def quality(x, goal): return 0.5 + 0.03 * sum(a == b for a, b in zip(x, goal))
def measure(x, goal, n): return sum(random.random() < quality(x, goal) for _ in range(n)) / n
def run(n, history):
    goal = [random.random() < .5 for _ in range(SIZE)]; tried = []
    for _ in range(STEPS * PER):
        if history and tried:                        # edit one of the top scorers
            parent = max(tried, key=lambda t: t[0])[1][:]; parent[random.randrange(SIZE)] ^= True
        else: parent = [random.random() < .5 for _ in range(SIZE)]
        tried.append((measure(parent, goal, n), parent))
    return quality(max(tried, key=lambda t: t[0])[1], goal)
random.seed(7)
for n in (30, 300):
    print(n, round(st.mean(run(n, True) for _ in range(150)), 3), round(st.mean(run(n, False) for _ in range(150)), 3))
# look for: history wins on the large scoring set and loses on the small one
# naive belief predicts: history wins at both sizes

Run on Python 3.15: at 300 examples true quality is 0.831 with history against 0.796 without; at 30, history loses, 0.719 against 0.743, because it keeps editing a lucky score. A toy shows the shape, not a size.

Measure it

  • Offline: test-set score of the final instruction against a named human baseline, and the gap between training and test. A wide gap means the search fit the sample.
  • In production: evaluations spent per point gained, per run. A curve that flattens for many rounds says stop.
  • Enforced by: a held-out gate in the release pipeline. Proposals are requests; the score decides, and the search has no brake unless you set a budget.

Interview

30-second answer: OPRO uses a model as the optimiser. Its prompt holds the task, a few exemplars and the best instructions so far with their scores, sorted ascending, and it asks for a new one that scores higher. You score it, add it and repeat. So the history is the context. Nothing is differentiated. Its reported gains are task maxima, on benchmarks with crisp answers.

Q · Mechanism — Why does putting scores in the prompt help? Because each proposal then conditions on what worked. The paper's ablation shows that dropping the scores does worse, and that ascending order beats descending. Its hypothesis for the order is recency: tokens near the end pull hardest.

Q · Trade-off — The paper reports up to 50% on Big-Bench Hard. Why isn't this everywhere? That figure is a maximum over tasks, not an expected gain, and a careful production prompt has less room. The simpler rung is a pool scored once, or a person with a set. OPRO costs many rounds of full evaluation, each returning one number. Today I'd take a reflective optimiser that reads failures.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Best zero-shot on GSM8K 80.2% PaLM 2-L scorer, "Take a deep breath…", 2023 cited (paper)
Human baseline 71.8% "Let's think step by step", same scorer cited (paper)
Gain, GSM8K up to 8% zero-shot, against human prompts cited (paper)
Gain, BBH up to 50% a maximum across BBH tasks cited (paper)

Pitfalls

  • 🧙 Folklore: "Tell the model to take a deep breath"
    ↳ Why it spread: it was the top line of a results table, and it's a fun sentence to repeat.
    ↳ What the evidence says: it topped GSM8K for one scorer, PaLM 2-L, in 2023. Other optimisers found other best lines, and it was scored at one position in the prompt.
    ↳ Do instead: treat a found instruction as specific to its model and task, and search your own.
  • "OPRO does gradient ascent on prompts"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the literature keeps using a gradient analogy.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: no derivative exists anywhere in it. Score-labelled text in a context lets a model continue a pattern, and that pattern can be wrong.
    ↳ Think instead: in-context conditioning on a history, not descent.
  • "A rising training curve means the prompt is improving"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the curve is the only thing the run draws, and it always trends upward, because it reports a running best.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the paper's own training scores were often 5–20 points above test, and a best-so-far line can't fall.
    ↳ Think instead: the training curve shows the search working; only a test score shows the prompt working.
  • Don't let the history grow, or run this with a human scoring.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: more history sounds like more signal, and a person is a good judge.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a long history costs tokens and buries its best lines in the middle, and a person can't afford eight scored sets per step.
    ↳ Do instead: keep the top few, score automatically, and cap the rounds. A person with a set is the simpler rung.
  • Shelf life: the specific found phrases are already stale. "Scores as context" stays as an idea.

Connections

Path:APEOPROTextGradevolutionary search
  • Builds on APE: the same scored selection, with memory.
  • Contrasts with TextGrad: a number per candidate against a written reason.
  • Measured by regression suites and CI: the held-out gate after the search.
  • Costed in cost-benefit: the rounds × set size bill.

notes.title: DSPy — Program the Pipeline, Compile the Prompts Against a Metric
notes.html:
References

Khattab et al. 2023: DSPy · DSPy docs: choosing an optimizer · DSPy docs: GEPA · DSPy docs: MIPROv2

TL;DR

You declare what goes in and out, pick a strategy, and supply a metric and data. An optimiser writes the prompt text. The source is the program, the set and the metric; the prompt is build output. A compile searches for whatever the metric rewards, so a bad metric gets faithfully optimised.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change
Flow:signaturemodulemetric + trainset + valsetoptimiser compilessaved programrun with compiled promptsrecompile

Recall

Prompt Answer
The three pieces? Signature (what), module (how), optimiser (the search that writes the text).
What does a compile change? Instructions and demonstrations, unless you choose a fine-tuning optimiser.
What is the source of truth? Program, data and metric. Compiled text is regenerated, not edited.

The idea

You have a three-step pipeline with a prompt string per step. The model changes, and every string was tuned to the old one. Somebody now spends a week re-tuning text, and nothing records why any phrase is there.

DSPy moves the prompt out of your source. You state a typed contract and choose a strategy such as chain-of-thought. An optimiser then runs your program, scores it with your metric and writes the text. On a new model you run that step again.

The metric is enforced; everything the prompt asks is still a request.

The trade: you give up direct control of the wording and accept a compile that is an inference bill, and you gain prompts you can regenerate from data.

How it works

The whole idea is a split between compile time and run time.

The model appears at compile time as well, so one compile can cost more than many requests.

Rule What actually happens
Start simple The docs call BootstrapFewShot "the safe first try" when the metric is reliable, and fine-tuning "the last lever".
MIPROv2 Bootstraps demos, proposes instructions from data and code, then runs a Bayesian search over combinations.
GEPA Tunes instructions from traces and written feedback, using a strong reflection model. It leads the docs' front page in 3.4.1.
Keep a test set GEPA without valset selects on trainset, which the docs say allows overfitting. Neither split is a final test.

Evolution

Lineage:Oct 2023 DSPy: teleprompters and bootstrappingJun 2024 MIPROJul 2025 GEPAAug 2026 dspy.Flex (experimental): rewriting a module's sourceOct 2026 3.4.1
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026). Releases are frequent, and 3.4.1 alone changed GEPA's default proposer.
  • Stronger-model test: no. Better models shrink the phrasing gain; re-deriving prompts per model is still useful. What won't change: the compile needs a metric that means what you want.

Code

The optimiser signature, on dspy 3.4.1. Numbers mark the pieces.

import dspy                                      # 3.4.1; dspy.GEPA needs Python < 3.15
TASK_MODEL, STRONG_MODEL = "…", "…"              # docs' reflection example, Oct 2026: openai/gpt-5.4
dspy.configure(lm=dspy.LM(TASK_MODEL))

class Triage(dspy.Signature):                    # ① the contract, with no prompt text
    """Classify a support ticket."""
    ticket: str = dspy.InputField()
    label: str = dspy.OutputField(desc="billing, bug, how-to or other")

def metric(gold, pred, trace=None, pred_name=None, pred_trace=None):   # ② the objective
    ok = pred.label == gold.label
    return dspy.Prediction(score=float(ok), feedback="" if ok else f"expected {gold.label}")

program = dspy.ChainOfThought(Triage)            # ③ the strategy
opt = dspy.GEPA(metric=metric, reflection_lm=dspy.LM(STRONG_MODEL), auto="light")   # ④ the search
compiled = opt.compile(program, trainset=train, valset=val)
compiled.save("triage.json")                     # ⑤ versioned, not edited

Break it: the belief that a compile finds the better prompt. Selection below uses a gameable metric.

outputs = {"plain": "Your refund was issued on 4 August.",
           "stuffed": "Refund refund policy: refund terms apply, see refund page for refund help."}
def metric(o): return o.lower().count("refund")          # "mentions the topic": gameable
def wanted(o): return "4 August" in o
best = max(outputs, key=lambda k: metric(outputs[k]))
print("compiler keeps:", best, "| what you wanted:", wanted(outputs[best]))
# look for: the candidate with the higher metric fails what you actually wanted
# naive belief predicts: the compiler finds the better prompt

Run on Python 3.15, it prints compiler keeps: stuffed | what you wanted: False. The selection step did its job; the metric was the bug.

Measure it

  • Offline: held-out metric and input tokens per call, compiled program against the hand-written baseline on the same model. Compiled prompts may carry more demos, so tokens belong in the comparison.
  • In production: quality and cost per compiled version. A drop with no compile means the model or the data moved.
  • Enforced by: the held-out gate before a compiled version ships. Inside the model, the compiled text is a request.

Interview

30-second answer: DSPy treats prompts as build output. I declare a signature, choose a module, and give it a metric and data. An optimiser then writes the instructions and demonstrations by running the program and scoring it. On a model change I recompile. So the valuable assets are the set and the metric, and the catch is that it optimises exactly what the metric rewards.

Q · Mechanism — What happens when you call compile? It depends on the optimiser. BootstrapFewShot runs the program and keeps passing traces as demos. MIPROv2 adds proposed instructions and a Bayesian search over combinations, scored on minibatches with periodic full checks. GEPA runs on a minibatch, reflects on traces and written feedback, proposes new instruction text and keeps a frontier of candidates. All of them return a program you save.

Q · Trade-off — When is DSPy the wrong choice? The simpler rung is a scored set with a person or fifty lines of candidate search. DSPy is wrong with no trusted metric, because then it's a wrapper plus a dependency. It's a poor fit where wording is reviewed or contractual, since the compiler rewrites it. And it's awkward for hotfixes, because a compile isn't a ten-minute step. I adopt it for stable multi-step pipelines that face repeated model changes.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
GSM8K quality 33% ─▶ 82% simple program to composed and compiled, GPT-3.5, 2023 cited (paper)
GSM8K quality 9% ─▶ 47% same comparison, llama2-13b-chat, 2023 cited (paper)
Pinned version dspy 3.4.1 released 12 Oct 2026 cited (volatile, as of Oct 2026)

Pitfalls

  • "DSPy is a prompt template library"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: you can see strings and fields, and it sits next to template tools.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a template manages text you wrote. Here the text is compile output from your program, data and metric. Pin most of it and you pay for machinery you've turned off.
    ↳ Think instead: if you are writing the prompt, you aren't using the compiler.
  • "The same seed gives the same compile"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: optimisers take a seed, so runs look reproducible.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the 3.4.1 release says GEPA results can differ from 3.4.0 with the same seed, because the default proposer changed. Provider models also change underneath.
    ↳ Think instead: pin the library version with the program, and keep the compiled file as the record.
  • Not the same: optimising prompts vs fine-tuning
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: DSPy does both, and "optimizer" and "training data" sound like weights.
    ↳ Difference: most optimisers change text in front of frozen weights. BootstrapFinetune and BetterTogether also touch weights, with training cost and deployment.
    ↳ Think instead: ask which variables a given optimiser changes.
  • Don't hand-edit a compiled prompt.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: during an incident, one changed line looks harmless.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the program and the artefact diverge, and the next compile discards the fix without telling anyone.
    ↳ Do instead: add the failure to the set and recompile, and keep a reviewed escape hatch for the outage.
  • Shelf life: optimiser names and defaults change within months (chapter map, Landscape). The compile and run split won't.

Connections

Path:OPRODSPyautomatic few-shot selectioncost-benefit
  • Builds on prompt chaining: the multi-step pipelines it compiles.
  • Measured by LLM as judge: often the metric, so validate it first.
  • Used by portability: recompiling is its answer to an upgrade.
  • Shipped by prompt versioning: compiled files are versioned like any prompt.
  • Drilled in what DSPy optimises.

notes.title: TextGrad — A Written Critique Passed Back Through the Pipeline
notes.html:
References

Yuksekgonul et al. 2024: TextGrad · TextGrad repository

TL;DR

A model critiques an output, and that critique is passed back to each upstream text variable, which is then revised. It says what was wrong, where a score only says how much.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change

Recall

Prompt Answer
What is the "gradient"? Written feedback from a model. Nothing is differentiated.
What does the API copy? PyTorch: variables, a loss, .backward(), an optimiser step.
Is 51% to 55% a prompt gain? No. It refines each answer at test time, GPQA, GPT-4o.

The idea

OPRO spends a scored set to learn one number. TextGrad spends a model call to learn a reason. The trade: more signal per run, and every step also trusts a critic's opinion. As a prompt optimiser, on gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 with gpt-4o as critic, it scored 91.9 against DSPy's 84.9 on Object Counting and tied on GSM8K and Word Sorting (2024).

Evolution

Lineage:Jun 2024 preprintMar 2025 NatureJul 2025 GEPA carries reflection into DSPy. 🔵 Emerging (Oct 2026): textgrad 0.1.8 is the latest PyPI release, from Mar 2025.

notes.title: Evolutionary Prompt Search — EvoPrompt and GEPA
notes.html:
References

Agrawal et al. 2025: GEPA · Guo et al. 2023: EvoPrompt

TL;DR

A model performs mutation and crossover on a population of prompts, and the eval score is the fitness. GEPA adds reflection on traces and keeps a Pareto frontier in place of one best prompt.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does the Pareto frontier keep? Any candidate best on at least one instance, so complementary lessons survive.
GEPA's aggregate gain? +13.33 against MIPROv2 +5.64, GPT-4.1 Mini, six benchmarks (2025).
Where did EvoPrompt struggle? OPRO's authors saw it degrade on GSM8K from generic starting prompts.

The idea

Keeping only the top prompt gets stuck. A population keeps variety, and GEPA's reflection reads why runs failed. The trade: fewer rollouts per gain, and you need a metric that writes useful feedback. Against GRPO on Qwen3 8B, GEPA gained 6% on average, up to 20%, with up to 35× fewer rollouts; GRPO still won on AIME-2025.

Evolution

Lineage:Sep 2023 EvoPromptJul 2025 GEPAICLR 2026 Oral. 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): dspy.GEPA leads the DSPy docs; standalone gepa is at 0.1.4 (Jul 2026). Use is in DSPy.

notes.title: Automatic Few-Shot Bootstrapping — Harvest Demonstrations From Runs That Passed
notes.html:
References

Opsahl-Ong et al. 2024: MIPRO · Khattab et al. 2023: DSPy · DSPy docs: BootstrapFewShot · DSPy docs: KNNFewShot

TL;DR

Run the program on labelled inputs, keep the runs the metric passes, and turn each module's real input and output into a demonstration. So every step gets examples of its own contract, which your end-to-end labels don't contain. The filter only sees the end of the run, so a kept demo can hide a bad middle step.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change
Flow:trainsetrun the programmetric on the final outputharvest each module's input and outputcandidate demo setssearch which setheld-out check

Recall

Prompt Answer
Bootstrapping vs selection? Bootstrapping generates demos by running; selection picks from labelled pairs.
Why does it matter for pipelines? Labels cover the ends; intermediate steps have no examples until the program runs.
Do demos beat instructions? Mostly in MIPRO's benchmarks; not on rule-heavy tasks, and it isn't a law.

The idea

A pipeline rewrites a query, retrieves, then reasons. Your labels are question and final answer. So what does a good input to the reasoning step look like? An expert would write tidy context; the real step receives retrieved chunks with headers and duplicates.

Bootstrapping gets that by running. Keep the runs that ended correctly, and each module's real traffic becomes its examples. Which examples to prefer stays with example selection; picking per request stays with retrieved few-shot. This note adds generating them and searching over sets against a metric.

Your code enforces which demos enter the prompt. That the model follows them is a request.

The trade: you spend compile-time calls and need a metric, and you get examples of real intermediate formats that nobody could write in advance.

How it works

The metric is the filter, and it runs at the end of the whole program.

Nothing inspects the middle of a run, which is the weakness Break it shows.

Source of demos Covers middle steps In the cached prefix Needs a metric
Hand-written guessed yes no
Selected from labels no yes to choose
Bootstrapped traces yes yes yes
Retrieved per request (KNNFewShot) through bootstrapping no not to retrieve
Fixed core + one retrieved yes the core for the core

Evolution

Lineage:2021 nearest-neighbour examplesOct 2023 DSPy BootstrapFewShotJun 2024 MIPRO: joint search2026 Google's optimizer offers demonstration mode
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026). A DSPy default, and offered by a provider tool.
  • Stronger-model test: partly. On GPT-4.1 Mini in 2025, instruction-only GEPA beat MIPROv2 with demos, so stronger models may lean less on examples. What won't change: a module's real format is known only by running it.
  • Checked on: Llama-3-8B (2024), Qwen3 8B and GPT-4.1 Mini (2025).

Code

The settings that matter, from dspy 3.4.1.

tp = dspy.BootstrapFewShot(metric=metric,        # an exact pass, or use metric_threshold for a score
                           max_bootstrapped_demos=4, max_labeled_demos=16, max_rounds=1)
compiled = tp.compile(program, trainset=train)   # defaults shown; a run is judged end to end

Break it: the belief that a kept demo is right at every step, on scripted runs.

runs = [
  {"q": "capital of france?", "gold": "Paris", "rewrite": "france capital", "answer": "Paris"},
  {"q": "capital of japan?",  "gold": "Tokyo", "rewrite": "japan capital",  "answer": "Tokyo, Japan"},
  {"q": "capital of peru?",   "gold": "Lima",  "rewrite": "weather in peru", "answer": "Lima"},
]
metric = lambda r: r["answer"] == r["gold"]                   # end-to-end exact match
print([(r["q"], r["rewrite"]) for r in runs if metric(r)])    # demos for the rewrite module
# look for: the bad 'weather in peru' rewrite kept, and the correct japan run dropped
# naive belief predicts: every kept demo is right at every step, and every right run is kept

Run on Python 3.15, it keeps the France and Peru rewrites and drops Japan. The bad rewrite became a demonstration because the last step happened to recover, and exact match threw away a good run.

Measure it

  • Offline: held-out score of compiled demos against the hand-written block, plus input tokens per call. Compare a few demo sets: MIPRO's authors saw high variation between sets.
  • In production: per-module input shape against the demos. A drift in the retriever's format means the demos are stale.
  • Enforced by: the metric as a filter at compile time, and the held-out gate. Reading the demos for personal data is a human review step.

Interview

30-second answer: Bootstrapping generates few-shot demos by running the program. Runs that pass the metric give each module examples of its real inputs and outputs. That solves a pipeline problem: labels exist only at the ends. An optimiser then searches over sets of demos. The catch is that the filter judges only the final output, so a lucky run can teach a bad intermediate step.

Q · Mechanism — Why is this better than using trainset examples directly? For one module, it isn't obviously better: your examples are already input-output pairs. In a pipeline, the labels have nothing about what a middle step should receive or emit. Running produces those, in the real format the previous step really emits. Keeping only passing runs is meant to propagate behaviour that worked end to end.

Q · Trade-off — Fixed bootstrapped demos, or retrieved per request? The simpler rung is a fixed block, and it wins operationally: it can sit in the cached prefix, it's deterministic, and it's a versioned artefact. Retrieval earns its place when inputs fall into clusters that need different examples, at the cost of the cache and an index. One design to test is a fixed core with one retrieved example below the breakpoint. I'd measure both accuracy and the cache loss.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Demos alone vs instructions alone demos won in all but one case Bootstrap Random Search vs best instruction-only, seven programs, Llama-3-8B, 2024 cited (paper)
The exception HotPotQA Conditional rule-heavy task: 0-shot instruction search won cited (paper)
Default caps 4 bootstrapped, 16 labelled BootstrapFewShot, dspy 3.4.1 cited (volatile, as of Oct 2026)

Pitfalls

  • "Demonstrations always matter more than the instruction"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: MIPRO's first lesson says so for most of its tasks, and it's a neat rule.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: conditional rules that a few examples can't express went the other way, and GEPA's instruction-only results beat demo-based runs on GPT-4.1 Mini.
    ↳ Think instead: it depends on whether the task's rules can be shown in a few examples, so test both.
  • Don't bootstrap from a set too small to hold out from.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: few labels exist, and every one looks useful as a demo.
    ↳ What goes wrong: demos drawn from the examples you score on look excellent and don't generalise. DSPy's guide warns that a demo set learned from 50 examples may not.
    ↳ Do instead: keep a set out of the run, and prefer instruction search on small sets.
  • Don't grow the demo count because compile allows it.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: each extra demo looks like free accuracy during the search.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every demo is input tokens on every request, and a longer block leaves more middle to lose.
    ↳ Do instead: price the tokens in the comparison. Fewer demos at the same held-out score win.
  • Not the same: bootstrapping vs dynamic retrieval
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: DSPy files KNNFewShot with the optimisers, so both look like compile steps.
    ↳ Difference: bootstrapping fixes demos at compile time. KNNFewShot searches on every forward call, so it adds work per request and changes the prompt each time.
    ↳ Think instead: ask when the choice is made, and who pays for it.
  • Shelf life: caps and optimiser names move. The missing labels for middle steps are permanent.

Connections

Path:example selectionDSPyautomatic few-shot bootstrappingcost-benefit
  • Builds on example selection: the axes a searched set still has to satisfy.
  • Contrasts with retrieved few-shot: chosen once, against chosen per request.
  • Measured by component vs end to end: why a passing run can hide a bad stage.
  • Attacked by indirect injection: harvested traces carry retrieved text into the prompt.
  • Costed in provider prompt caching: what a fixed block saves.

notes.title: Prompt Distillation — Move a Long Prompt Into Fewer Tokens or Into the Weights
notes.html:
References

Snell et al. 2022: Learning by Distilling Context · OpenAI: deprecations

TL;DR

Run the model with the long context, collect its outputs, then fine-tune it to give them without that context. Behaviour moves from text to weights, so each later change is a training run.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change

Recall

Prompt Answer
The two directions? Fewer tokens (compression), or into weights (context distillation).
What do you give up? Changing behaviour by editing text.
Try first? Prompt caching: the prefix stays editable.

The idea

You pay for the same long prompt on every request. Distillation pays once, offline. On SPIDER text-to-SQL with Incoder-6.7B (2022), the student reached 27.9 from eight in-context examples, close to the teacher's 28.2, against 18.9 for direct gradient descent. The trade: cheaper requests for a frozen behaviour.

Evolution

Lineage:Sep 2022 context distillationOct 2023 LLMLingua compression. ⚪ Fading (Oct 2026): caching comes first, and OpenAI ends new fine-tuning jobs for active customers on 6 Jan 2027.

notes.title: Cost-Benefit of Auto-Optimisation — Price the Run Against How Long the Gain Lasts
notes.html:
References

DSPy docs: choosing an optimizer · DSPy docs: MIPROv2 · Agrawal et al. 2025: GEPA · Opsahl-Ong et al. 2024: MIPRO

TL;DR

A compile is an inference workload, so you can count its calls before starting. The benefit is a held-out gain × the requests served before the model or the task changes. So optimise what is stable and high-volume; the set and the metric pay for themselves whether you run an optimiser or not.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change
Flow:trusted metric?failures about wording?stable for months?traffic repays the run?count the callsrunheld-out gateship until the next model change

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does a run cost? Program runs × model calls per run × tokens × price, plus proposal calls.
What term decides most cases? How long the prompt stays valid, because a model change resets it.
What survives a skipped run? The set and the metric: gate, upgrade test and search target.

The idea

A team has two hours of compute or a week of an engineer. Then someone reads fifty failures and finds the retriever returning wrong chunks, which no search over wording can reach.

An optimiser buys the last points once the structure is right; an engineer buys the structure and the harness, and they come in that order.

The budget is enforced only if you set one in code. "Keep it cheap" is not a control.

The trade: a fixed inference bill and a review of text nobody wrote, for a bounded gain that expires at the next model change.

How it works

Each gate zeroes one term of the benefit. This tree owns "should I run one?"; the chapter map owns "which one?".

Only the last gate needs arithmetic. Here it is, for MIPROv2 as dspy 3.4.1 estimates it. The per-call sum belongs to cost modelling.

runs    = m · T + V · (⌊T / s⌋ + 1)    ← m minibatch, T trials, V val set, full check every s trials
calls   = runs · M + proposals         ← M model calls per program run
cost    = calls · t · r                ← t tokens per call, r price per token
benefit = Q · Δv                       ← Q requests before the next change, Δv held-out value each
Rule What actually happens
Minibatching cuts the bill MIPROv2 scores trials on 35 examples by default, with a full check every 5 trials.
A cheap search model has a catch Searching on a small model saves money, but the winner must be re-scored on the production model (portability).
Compile once, reuse DSPy's guide notes that the cost amortises over a saved program.

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026). Frameworks ship budget presets, and rollouts per gain is now a headline axis in papers.
  • Stronger-model test: a stronger model may shrink Δv, because less is left to find. What won't change: benefit is bounded by how long the result stays valid.

Code

Break it: the belief that the smallest preset is a quick check, for a 3-module program.

import math
def mipro_runs(predictors, n, val, minibatch=35, every=5):      # dspy 3.4.1 MIPROv2 presets
    trials = int(max(2 * predictors * 2 * math.log2(n), 1.5 * n))
    return trials, minibatch * trials + val * (trials // every + 1)
for name, n, val in (("light", 6, 100), ("medium", 12, 300), ("heavy", 18, 1000)):
    t, runs = mipro_runs(3, n, val)
    print(f"{name}: {t} trials, {runs} program runs, {runs * 3} model calls")
# look for: thousands of model calls from the smallest preset on a 3-module program
# naive belief predicts: `light` is a quick local check

Run on Python 3.15, it prints the rows in Numbers, from the dspy 3.4.1 source formulas. Proposal calls come on top.

Measure it

  • Offline: held-out gain against the hand-tuned baseline, beside the run's real calls and tokens. A gain inside the noise floor makes the run a loss, however cheap.
  • In production: spend per compile, and days from compile to the next model change. Short lives mean the validity term is failing.
  • Enforced by: a budget set in code, such as auto or max_metric_calls on GEPA, and the held-out gate. The tree itself is a decision, not a control.

Interview

30-second answer: A compile is an inference job: trials, set size and calls per run multiply out to thousands of calls. The benefit is a bounded gain that lasts until the next model change. So I ask four things in order: do I trust the metric, are failures about wording, is it stable, and does the traffic repay it? The harness is worth building even if the answer is no.

Q · Mechanism — How would you size a run before starting it? I count program runs: trials times minibatch, plus full checks on the validation set. Then I multiply by model calls per run and tokens per call, and add proposal calls. For MIPROv2's light preset on a three-module program with 100 validation examples, that's 1,785 program runs, or 5,355 task-model calls. I date the price the day I check it, and I set the cap in code.

Q · Trade-off — When is a week of an engineer better than a two-hour run? When the problem isn't in the prompt, or no metric exists. The simpler rung, a person reading failures, finds a missing tool or bad retrieval, and that's usually worth more than a search can extract. The week also builds the set, which every later decision uses. The run wins in a narrow case: a mature program, a trusted metric, a stable model and traffic that makes a few points matter.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
light 5,355 calls 3 modules: 31 trials, 1,785 runs, val 100 derived, dspy 3.4.1 source
medium 12,615 calls 3 modules: 43 trials, 4,205 runs, val 300 derived, dspy 3.4.1 source
heavy 38,250 calls 3 modules: 50 trials, 12,750 runs, val 1,000 derived, dspy 3.4.1 source
GEPA run size 1,839–7,051 rollouts six benchmarks, Qwen3 8B, 2025; GRPO used 24,000 cited (paper)
GEPA money "hundreds of dollars per run" possible DSPy's guide, as of Oct 2026 cited (volatile, as of Oct 2026)

Pitfalls

  • "Auto-optimisation is cheap, it's only a script"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the code is three lines, and the preset is called light.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: three lines start thousands of model calls, as Break it counts. It's cheap against an engineer-week, which is a different comparison from free.
    ↳ Think instead: budget a compile like any batch job, before you start it.
  • Don't optimise a prompt that changes weekly.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the prompt getting the most attention, so it feels like the priority.
    ↳ What goes wrong: each change invalidates the run, so Q in the benefit sum stays small and the gain never repays the bill.
    ↳ Do instead: hand-tune with a scored set until it settles.
  • Don't start with an optimiser before the failure analysis.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a two-hour run looks cheaper than a week of reading.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the search can't add a tool or fix retrieval, so you get a small gain on the wrong problem, plus text nobody can review.
    ↳ Do instead: take the simpler rung: read failures, fix structure, then search.
  • Not the same: an optimiser's gain vs its ROI
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: a paper reports the gain, and a team reads it as the case for adopting.
    ↳ Difference: the gain is a benchmark maximum on the paper's model. ROI is your held-out gain × your traffic × your prompt's life, minus the run.
    ↳ Think instead: a number from a paper is only ever a reason to test.
  • Shelf life: preset sizes and prices move. The shape of the sum doesn't.

Connections

  • Measured by regression suites and CI: the held-out gate.
  • Breaks when combined with judge biases: a biased judge as metric gets amplified.

notes.title: Portability of Optimised Prompts — The Winner Was Fitted to One Model
notes.html:
References

Agrawal et al. 2025: GEPA · Yang et al. 2023: OPRO · Google: data-driven optimizer · Anthropic: prompting best practices

TL;DR

An optimiser's winner is a maximum over one model's scores, so some of its gain belongs to that model. Some of it transfers and some doesn't, and you find out only by re-scoring. So store which model it was fitted to, re-score it unchanged, and recompile only if it really regressed.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery change
Flow:new modelre-score the compiled prompt unchangedkeep and record
remove model-specific clausesre-scorerecompile from the set and metricheld-out gate

Recall

Prompt Answer
Does an optimised prompt transfer? Partly. Measure it. GEPA: +9.00 moved, against +12.19 fitted directly, in one test.
What survives an upgrade? Program, set and metric. The measured gain doesn't.
The field a compiled prompt must carry? The model it was optimised on.

The idea

The idea that a shipped prompt is a tuple is owned by the prompt as a coupled system. An optimised prompt adds a sharper problem. A hand-written prompt has reasons you can read. A compiled one has none: nobody knows which clause carries the gain, so you can't edit it for a new model by reasoning about it.

Part of what the search rewarded is meaning, and part is what prompt sensitivity calls features that shouldn't matter. Part may be a clause that compensated for one model's habit.

The trade: recompiling for each model pays the search bill again; skipping it keeps a prompt whose gain is an old measurement.

How it works

This is the part of an upgrade specific to compiled prompts. The whole migration is owned by model-upgrade migration.

Recompiling is the last step, not the first, because the bill comes only when a measurement asks for it.

Part of the artefact On a model change
Program, set, metric survive unchanged
Compiled instructions keep only if a re-score says so
Bootstrapped demos they show the old model's outputs, so they are the first thing to regenerate
The measured gain void: it describes a pair of model and prompt that no longer exists

Evolution

Lineage:Sep 2023 OPRO: found instructions differ per scorerOct 2023 DSPy: recompile per modelJul 2025 GEPA: a cross-model row2026 Google's optimizer: a source_model setting for upgrades
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026). Recompiling is standard advice, and evidence on how much transfers is thin: one row in one paper.
  • Stronger-model test: no. Providers keep retiring models, so a compiled prompt always meets one it wasn't fitted to. What won't change: a score belongs to a pair of model and prompt.
  • Checked on: Qwen3 8B to GPT-4.1 Mini (2025). Transfer between other pairs is untested here.

Code

The fields a compiled prompt adds to the tuple record.

compiled_from: { program: triage@v7, dspy: 3.4.1, optimizer: GEPA, auto: light }
optimised_on: "{{pinned model snapshot}}"
trainset: golden/triage-train@v4
heldout: golden/triage-heldout@v4     # score below is on this set only
heldout_score: "{{measured}}"

Break it: the belief that any drop after an upgrade means recompile. The noise band decides; the paired version is in error bars and paired tests.

import math
def triage(old, new, n, z=2):                     # old and new: pass rates on the same n cases
    p = (old + new) / 2
    band = z * math.sqrt(2 * p * (1 - p) / n)     # unpaired, so wider than a paired test
    return "regressed" if new < old - band else "improved" if new > old + band else "within noise"
for n in (100, 2000):
    print(n, triage(0.80, 0.75, n))
# look for: the same 5-point drop is noise on 100 cases and a regression on 2,000
# naive belief predicts: any drop after an upgrade means recompile

Run on Python 3.15, it prints within noise for 100 cases and regressed for 2,000. A compile triggered by the first would pay to chase noise.

Measure it

  • Offline: held-out score of the unchanged compiled prompt on the new model, against the same prompt on the old model and against a recompiled one. Baseline: the old pair.
  • In production: the share of compiled prompts whose optimised_on is no longer the live model. That is your stale inventory.
  • Enforced by: the gate that blocks a model change until each compiled prompt has a recorded score on it. A missing optimised_on should fail the check.

Interview

30-second answer: An optimised prompt is a maximum over one model's scores, so part of its gain may not move. There's some evidence it can: GEPA's prompt, optimised on Qwen3, kept most of its gain on GPT-4.1 Mini. So I don't assume either way. I record the model it was fitted to, re-score it unchanged on the new one, and recompile from the set and metric only if it truly regressed.

Q · Mechanism — Why might a good optimised prompt fall on a better model? Because the score rewarded more than meaning. The search also absorbs format effects that were specific to that model, and clauses that compensated for its habits. Anthropic's guide, as of Oct 2026, tells migrating users to reduce old anti-laziness prompting, because newer Claude models may overtrigger on it. A clause written to correct one model becomes an instruction to the next.

Q · Trade-off — Would you recompile everything at every upgrade? No. The simpler rung is an unchanged re-score, which is one eval run per prompt, and it may show nothing is needed. Next comes deleting model-specific clauses, which costs almost nothing. Only what remains gets a recompile. Recompiling everything pays the whole bill, changes prompts that were fine, and moves many things at once, so a regression can't be attributed.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Fitted directly on GPT-4.1 Mini +12.19 (GEPA), +13.33 (GEPA+Merge) aggregate over six benchmarks, 2025 cited (paper)
Fitted on Qwen3 8B, run on GPT-4.1 Mini +9.00 same benchmarks, no modification cited (paper)
MIPROv2 fitted on GPT-4.1 Mini +5.64 same table cited (paper)
Share of the direct gain kept 74% (of +12.19) 9.00 / 12.19, one pair of models derived

Pitfalls

  • "Optimised prompts never transfer"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the argmax argument is clean, and it became a slogan.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the argument says there's no guarantee, not that transfer fails. GEPA's cross-model row beat optimisers fitted directly to the target model.
    ↳ Think instead: portability is a measurement, not a property you can assume in either direction.
  • "A better model does at least as well on the same prompt"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: better on average sounds like better everywhere.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: an average says nothing about your prompt, and clauses written for the old model's faults now act as instructions.
    ↳ Think instead: re-score each prompt; the new model's benchmark isn't your eval.
  • Don't search on a cheap model and ship to an expensive one on trust.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it cuts the run's bill, and one paper shows it working.
    ↳ What goes wrong: that result is one pair of models. On your pair it may not hold, and you'd never know.
    ↳ Do instead: use it for the search, then score the winner on the production model.
  • Don't recompile every prompt at once.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a single upgrade project feels tidier than a triage.
    ↳ What goes wrong: forty prompts moving together make any regression impossible to attribute, and most may have needed nothing.
    ↳ Do instead: take the simpler rung, a re-score per prompt, and canary per prompt.
  • Shelf life: how much transfers will change with each generation. Recording the fitted model won't.
